summary: A periodic index-style memo that summarizes the RFCs published in the range 2800 through 2899. Like others in its series, it is a reference aid for finding documents in the series, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a librarian making a short list of every book added to one shelf. This is that list for one hundred RFC documents.

questions: how to find an rfc on a topic
subtitle: An index and summary of 100 RFCs published between RFC 2800 and RFC 2899.

tldr.problem: A hundred RFCs were published in the series 2800-2899, covering diverse topics from cryptography to telephony. Readers need a quick overview of what each document is about.
tldr.mechanism: This memo provides a chronologically organized annotated list of all 100 RFCs in the series, with each RFC's authors, publication date, title, and a brief summary of its content.
tldr.outcome: Readers can quickly scan the entire series to find documents relevant to their interest, without searching the full RFC database.

today: RFC 2899 is an Informational memo published in May 2001 as a finding aid for RFCs 2800 through 2899. Similar summary memos exist for other ranges of RFCs (such as RFC 1000 for RFCs 1-99, RFC 2000 for RFCs 1900-1999, and RFC 3000 for RFCs 2900-2999). These summary memos are no longer actively maintained as the RFC series has grown to over 9000 documents, but they remain useful historical references.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
RFC 2899 is a summary index of RFCs 2800 through 2899, a series of 100 documents published by the Internet community. This memo provides a quick reference guide to all documents in that range, allowing readers to see at a glance what topics are covered and which RFCs might be relevant to their work.

The document follows a format established by earlier summary memos in the series. Each RFC is listed chronologically with its authors, publication date, title, and a brief description of its scope. Some RFCs are marked as being on the standards track, meaning they are Proposed Standards, Draft Standards, or full Internet Standards; others are Informational memos (like this one) or Best Current Practices (BCPs).
sections.plainLanguage: This document is an index: a table of contents with short descriptions. It helps you find which RFC covers a topic you care about.

sections.title: Topics Covered in This Range
sections.content:
The RFCs in the 2800-2899 range (published from 2000 to 2001) cover a broad spectrum of Internet technologies. The series includes cryptography and security standards (PKCS #5, key exchange algorithms), network protocols (IPv6 mechanisms, DNS extensions), routing and telephony (TRIP framework, MGCP audio packages), media access and switching (LAN switching benchmarks, SRP MAC protocol), authentication and accounting (RADIUS extensions and accounting), and operational standards (root nameserver requirements, NAS practices).

Some documents define new protocol features or extensions, while others provide guidance on implementation, analysis, or best practices. The range illustrates the breadth of the RFC publication process and the diverse concerns of the Internet community at the turn of the millennium.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFCs in this range cover security, routing, audio, network protocols, and many other internet topics. It is a snapshot of what the internet community was working on around 2000-2001.

sections.title: Standards Track RFCs in the Series
sections.content:
Within the 2800-2899 range, a significant subset of documents are on the standards track. These RFCs have undergone review and discussion within the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) and represent proposed or adopted standards for Internet protocols and practices.

Examples in this range include RFC 2891 (LDAP sorting), RFC 2890 (GRE extensions), RFC 2894 (Router Renumbering for IPv6), RFC 2893 (IPv6 transition mechanisms), RFC 2885 and 2886 (Megaco protocol and errata), RFC 2883 (TCP SACK extension), RFC 2879 (Internet Fax content features), and RFC 2878 (PPP Bridging Control Protocol). These documents define protocol behaviors and requirements that implementations should follow to ensure interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Some RFCs in this range are official standards that all implementations should follow. Others are just proposals or informational guides.

sections.title: Informational and Guidance Memos
sections.content:
A significant portion of the 2800-2899 range consists of Informational memos, which provide information or describe protocols without establishing Internet standards. Examples include RFC 2892 (Cisco SRP MAC protocol), RFC 2897 (MGCP Advanced Audio proposal), RFC 2889 (LAN switching benchmarking methodology), RFC 2887 (reliable multicast design space), and RFC 2871 (telephony routing framework).

Best Current Practices (BCPs) in this range offer operational and implementation guidance for network administrators and protocol developers. RFC 2870 provides operational requirements for root nameservers. These documents, while not establishing mandatory standards, provide valuable guidance and context for implementation and deployment decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: Not all RFCs are strict rules. Many are proposals, guidance, or interesting ideas. They help the community understand new areas but are not requirements.

sections.title: How to Use This Index
sections.content:
This memo is organized chronologically, listing RFCs in descending order from 2899 down to 2800. Each entry shows the RFC number, author name(s), publication date, title, and a one or two sentence summary of the RFC's content. To find RFCs on a specific topic, scan the titles and summaries or use the document's table of contents.

For each RFC listed, the full text is available from the RFC Editor website (www.rfc-editor.org) and other RFC repositories. If a document is marked [STANDARDS TRACK], you can check the Internet Official Protocol Standards document (STD 1) for its current status (Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, or Internet Standard). This memo itself is Informational and serves as a finding aid rather than a specification or requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: To use this, scan the list until you find a title that interests you, then read the RFC itself from the official RFC website.
